A man named Aaron Vale sits in an office while a doctor explains the numbers on a screen, showing that his heart will fail within weeks unless a donor is found. Somewhere else, an ex-convict named Wes Tarrow, recently born again, coaches a boys' baseball team on Saturdays, shouting instructions while his wife, Nita, watches from the bleachers, quietly fearing the volatile fanaticism that still simmers inside him.

In a bathroom stall, Lena Ward locks the door and snorts cocaine, returning to the habit she abandoned long ago. She stands at a kitchen table surrounded by her daughters' drawings, having already been taken into a quiet hospital side room where a doctor told her that a runaway pickup truck struck her husband, Doug, and both their little girls at a crossing, killing them all. 

At a motel four hundred miles from his old life, Wes cleans rooms. He had walked out on his early parole, abandoning both Nita and his faith at the prison gate. Inside a dimly lit room nearby, Lena demands that the driver who shattered her world be killed. Aaron, sitting beside her, buys a pistol from a man in a lock-up and drives out to the motel to find the desk clerk.

Before the accident, Lena Ward lived a quiet, settled suburban life with Doug and their two young daughters, secure in a routine devoid of the addictions that once plagued her. Across town, a private investigator handed Aaron a piece of paper with Lena’s name and address on it, taking cash in a parking garage to violate confidentiality rules. Aaron, driven by an obsession to find the widow of the man whose heart now beat in his chest, followed Lena for a week, engineered a meeting at a public swimming pool, and began an affair with her.

When the pickup struck Doug and the two girls, Wes had paused a hundred yards down the road, backed up, and then fled into the night. Driven by guilt, he eventually walked into a police station, confessed to the hit-and-run, and returned to prison.

In a hospital operating room, surgeons opened Aaron’s chest and transplanted Doug’s heart into him, allowing Aaron to wake up breathing easily for the first time in months. Later, in Lena's kitchen, Aaron confessed that he was carrying her late husband's heart inside him. She threw him out into the night, only to call him back four days later.

Before his illness took its final toll, Aaron sat across a kitchen table from his estranged wife, Della. She pushed a clinic consent form toward him, begging him to agree to posthumous insemination using his frozen sperm before he died. Months later, after beginning his affair with Lena, Aaron left Della for good, declaring he wanted no part of the child she was trying to conceive.

Behind the motel, Aaron cornered Wes in the dark, pointing the pistol at him. Unable to pull the trigger to kill, Aaron fired a shot that merely wounded Wes, shouting at the ex-convict to run. Instead, bleeding through his shirt, Wes followed Aaron and Lena back to their motel room and stood in the doorway, begging Aaron to finish the job. Aaron turned the gun on himself and pulled the trigger, shooting himself directly in the chest.

Lena and Wes hauled the dying Aaron into a car and sped toward a hospital with the horn blaring, but on the operating table, the transplanted heart finally failed. Wes returned home to the family he had walked away from, while Lena, carrying Aaron's unborn child, returned home alone.

The robbery collapsed within a minute. Bullets shredded the glass as Mr. Ash shot their way clear of the police from the getaway car, with Mr. Elm gasping in the passenger seat beside him. Fleeing on foot after the car died, Elm hijacked a vehicle, but the terrified driver pulled a pistol from her door pocket and shot him in the stomach before Elm shot her dead and sped off. Ash drove the screaming, bleeding Elm to the warehouse rendezvous, cradling him on the cold floor and swearing he was not going to die today.

Months before the blood ran across the concrete, undercover officer Danny Roarke had sat in a windowless room with his handler, Pruitt. They rehearsed a fabricated anecdote about a drug bust in a public toilet over and over, until Danny could tell it with the unforced rhythm of a genuine memory. When Danny performed the story for the boss, Bram, his son Cal, and Ash, they bought it completely, bringing him onto the crew under the mantle of Mr. Elm.

In the dim warehouse, Mr. Birch arrived clean and furious. He argued bitterly that the job was an inside setup, compromised by an informer, before slipping outside alone to hide the diamonds where no eyes could trace them.

Before any of them had worn black suits, Ren Vasco had walked out of prison after years of silence, reporting straight to Bram and Cal to collect on the debt they owed him. The full crew had later gathered over breakfast, squabbling about what a pop song really meant and whether waitresses deserved a tip, right before Bram handed out tree aliases from a list and Birch loudly complained about his assigned name.

Cedar strolled into the warehouse unhurried, pulling a kidnapped patrolman named Doyle from the boot of his car. Left alone with the bound officer, Cedar turned up a radio oldie, danced a few steps, sliced off Doyle’s ear with a razor, and doused him in petrol. From his place on the floor, Elm summoned his remaining strength and shot Cedar dead. Elm whispered to the terrified Doyle that he was a cop and that the force was waiting outside for Bram. But when Cal returned, he listened to Elm’s cover story about Cedar going wild, accepted it, and calmly put three rounds into Doyle himself to eliminate the witness.

Bram walked in moments later, surveyed the bodies, and immediately named Elm as the informer. Ash, bound by the bond of carrying his dying friend inside, refused to believe Bram and drew his gun on his own boss instead. The tense three-way standoff exploded into gunfire, leaving Bram and Cal dead, Ash mortally wounded, and Elm barely breathing in his own pooling blood.

Bleeding out beside him, Elm finally confessed the truth to Ash: he really was a police officer. Stunned by the confession, Ash dragged himself up, pressed his pistol to Elm’s head, and fired just as the police battered through the warehouse doors and cut Ash down in a hail of bullets.

Hitmen Rollo and Marcus drove across the city, debating foreign drug laws and what fast food is called abroad. Waiting in the corridor outside their target’s flat, they argued over whether a foot massage was worth killing a man for. Inside, Marcus recited a passage of scripture before he and Rollo shot a young man named Tobin for double-crossing their employer, Otis, and recovered a stolen briefcase. Seconds later, a fourth man hidden in the bathroom emptied a revolver at them without hitting either, which Marcus called divine intervention. In the car afterward, Rollo’s gun accidentally went off over a bump, blowing the head off their passenger, Del. Marcus parked the bloodied car at his friend Warren’s house, where a soft-spoken fixer directed the cleanup and dressed both men in borrowed shorts and T-shirts. Later, over breakfast in a coffee shop, two small-time robbers decided on the spot to hold up the diner. When a pistol was thrust in his face, Marcus talked the robber down mid-holdup, handed over his own wallet, kept the briefcase, and let the couple walk out. The two hitmen then delivered the briefcase to Otis at his bar, where Otis was paying an ageing boxer named Denny to take a dive in the fifth round.

Rollo bought a bag of unusually pure heroin from his dealer Kip and shot up at the kitchen table before his night out. He took Otis’s wife, Nadia, to a themed diner where they took off their shoes and won the dance contest. Back at her flat, Nadia found the bag in Rollo’s coat, mistook it for cocaine, and snorted a line. She overdosed on the carpet and was revived only by a needle of adrenaline driven straight into her heart on the dealer’s living-room floor.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war sat a young boy named Denny down in a bare front room and put into his hands the gold watch his father had kept hidden through years of captivity. 

Decades later, Denny refused to go down in the fifth. He double-crossed Otis, winning the fight and hitting his opponent hard enough to kill him in the ring before escaping in a passing taxi. Hiding in a motel on the edge of town with his girlfriend Marielle, Denny discovered she had left his father’s watch behind on the bedside table in his flat. Denny returned for the watch and found it, but as Rollo emerged from the bathroom, Denny grabbed a submachine gun left on the kitchen counter and shot the hitman dead. Driving away, Denny collided with Otis in the street, wrecking both cars, and both men were dragged down into the basement of a pawnshop by the twisted shopkeepers. Denny broke free of his restraints and made it to the door, but stopped, pulled a sword down off the shop wall, and went back to rescue Otis while one of their captors was raping him. Afterward, Otis declared them square on the condition that Denny leave town forever. Denny collected Marielle from the motel, put her on the back of a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop, and rode out of the city with the watch back on his wrist.

Before the darkness broke him, insurance investigator Martin Kray sat behind a desk, putting a soft-spoken claimant named Elias Prine through ruthless battery tests. Martin ruled the man’s sudden memory loss psychosomatic and denied the claim. Left without care, Elias’s diabetic wife tested her husband’s condition herself, placing her watch forward and begging for insulin injection after injection. Elias administered every dose as if it were the first, until she died of an overdose he could never recall giving her.

Months later, Martin walked into a tattoo parlour, clutch of scrap paper in hand. He watched the needle etch a vehicle registration down his thigh, placing it directly beneath the five unshakeable facts already carved into his flesh. He did not remember writing the note that ordered it, only that his own handwriting was the single truth he possessed.

The night two intruders burst through his bathroom door, Martin shot one across his wife’s fallen body before the second smashed his head into the mirror. His wife died, and Martin’s ability to retain new memories vanished forever. To survive, he built an elaborate system of captioned polaroids, taped index cards, and tattooed facts.

In her bar, a woman named Corinne watched Martin walk in wearing a tailored suit she recognized and park a sleek sports car she knew well. Smiling coldly, she poured him a beer that her staff had quietly spat into, watching the stranger drink down her dead boyfriend’s life.

A year before, a plainclothes officer named Roy had guided Martin to a ruined building, standing by while Martin killed the real attacker—a vengeance Martin forgot within minutes. Now, sitting on a cheap motel bed, Martin recited the Prine case over the phone to an anonymous voice. Afterwards, in a vacant field, he burned his late wife’s hairbrush and paperbacks, trying to mourn a loss his mind refused to keep.

Back at her house, Corinne hid every pen. She goaded Martin until he struck her, then waited outside for the bruises to bloom before returning to blame a man named Vance. Armed with a stranger's grudge, Martin ambushed Vance in a motel bathroom, beat him bloody, and forced him out of town at gunpoint.

The anonymous caller gave Martin a name and address: a drug dealer named Gil Marsh. Martin tracked Gil to a derelict basement, strangled him with a leather belt, and photographed the corpse. As he suffocated, Gil gasped out a single word—"Elias"—before going limp. Ignorant of its meaning, Martin stripped the body, dressed in Gil’s suit, and drove off in his sports car.

Corinne ran the registration plate from Martin’s forgotten notes through a contact at the vehicle registry. She handed him the official printout across a table, revealing the owner's full name: Roy Mercer.

Roy found Martin soon after Gil’s death, explaining the bitter truth: Gil was innocent, the real killer had died a year ago by Roy’s own assistance, and the tragic story Martin told strangers was his own shattered life. Refusing a reality that left him with no purpose, Martin burned his photos of Gil, scribbled HE IS LYING TO YOU across Roy’s photograph, and copied down Roy’s license plate as his next target.

Martin lured Officer Roy Mercer back to the derelict building under a false pretense. As the officer stepped inside, Martin raised his gun, put a bullet through Roy’s head, and snapped a picture of the corpse, entirely satisfied that he had carried out the truth written in his own hand.

On his twenty-fifth birthday, Emmett Rusk officially inherited his immense fortune. As the banker Barrow read aloud the long list of holdings, Emmett casually announced that out of all of them, he wanted to run the loss-making city newspaper, the Clarion, simply because he thought it might be fun. 

He promptly moved a bed into the newspaper’s offices, setting up his manager Marsh and his childhood friend Devlin on either side of him. On the front page, over his own signature, Emmett printed a bold declaration of principles promising what the paper would always deliver. To secure its future, he bought out the rival newspaper’s entire staff by offering double their wages, celebrating the acquisition with a lavish party complete with a brass band and a chorus line, dancing joyously in the center of the room.

Years earlier, in a cramped western mining boarding house, a lodger unable to pay his rent had left behind a seemingly worthless mine deed. When a vast seam of gold was discovered beneath the claim, Emmett’s mother signed her young son and the fortune over to the eastern banker Barrow at the kitchen table, while the boy's father protested uselessly from the doorway. 

When Barrow walked down the snow-covered steps to collect him, the boy slammed his sled straight into the banker’s stomach, knocking him down into the snow. But no matter how hard he fought, the child was hauled into the carriage and taken east that very night.

Now a wealthy adult, Emmett returned from a European buying trip loaded with classical statuary and engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. Their wedding dominated every front page except his own. Yet the marriage quickly turned hollow. Across a sequence of silent breakfasts, the dining table grew longer and the conversation shorter, until Emmett and Adele sat at opposite ends, hiding behind competing newspapers.

One afternoon, after being splashed by a passing cab, Emmett stood laughing at the mud on his coat outside a chemist's shop. Nora Kell, a shopgirl nursing a toothache, laughed back. Before long, Emmett was secretly visiting her private rooms.

Midway through Emmett’s campaign for governor, party boss Halloran escorted Adele up the stairs to Nora’s flat, offering a blunt ultimatum: withdraw on grounds of ill health, or face public exposure by Monday morning. Emmett told Halloran to get out.

Emmett lost the election, while the Clarion ran "FRAUD AT THE POLLS" across six columns. Devlin asked to be transferred to another city, and Adele departed without a word. 

Determined to remake his image, Emmett married Nora and forced her into an opera career. He hired the finest vocal coach and built a grand opera house specifically for her, insisting the public treat her as a star. Nora’s debut was an absolute humiliation. Devlin, brought back to cover the performance, got drunk rather than write a cruel review and passed out over half a paragraph. Emmett finished the savage review himself, printed it on the front page, and fired his oldest friend.

Unable to face another night on stage, Nora swallowed poison. Finding her in her darkened bedroom, Emmett finally relented and let her quit singing. He shut her away in Silvermount, a cavernous, half-finished mountain palace, where she spent empty days assembling jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall as large as a train station. After a joyless beach picnic and a bitter quarrel, Nora packed her bags and left him, ignoring his furious demands that she stay.

Enraged, Emmett tore Nora’s bedroom apart with his hands. He stopped only when his fingers brushed a small glass snow globe. He murmured a single word—"Bluebell"—and carried the toy past facing mirrors that reflected his aging image into infinity.

In an upstairs bed at Silvermount, Emmett murmured "Bluebell" one last time, releasing the globe to shatter on the floor as he died alone.

A nine-minute newsreel obituary recapped his public life, leaving his final utterance completely unexplained. A reporter named Nash was assigned to uncover its meaning, but when he tracked Nora down in a seaside nightclub, the drunken former singer turned him away. 

Nash read Barrow’s memoirs and interviewed Marsh, Devlin, Nora, and the old butler Colm. Finding no answers, Nash snapped his notebook shut, remarking that no single word could ever explain a man's life—unaware that down in the cellar, workmen clearing Silvermount's crates were shoveling a boy's small wooden sled, stenciled with the word *Bluebell*, into the roaring furnace.

Tobias woke with a hollow headache, stripped of two years he could not name. On an unreasoned impulse, he skipped work, boarded the train to the end of the rail line, and walked onto the frozen sand, where a woman with dyed hair stood waiting as if by design.

Years earlier, that same train line had brought them together at a seaside beach party. They had broken the window of an empty shore house to sleep on bare floorboards, inaugurating two years of fierce devotion—lying out on the ice of the frozen river, huddled in the steam of a noodle house, and sharing quiet laughter in the back seat at the drive-in.

Now, driving back into the city, they talked with an immediate, inexplicable ease. Outside her building, she invited him up to her flat for a drink as naturally as if they had known each other forever.

Yet before the blankness, that closeness had curdled into venom. Her drinking had clashed against his tight-lipped withholding until she came home drunk with a dented car. The resulting fight broke them for good, and Ivy walked straight to a shabby clinic, paying Dr. Hallam to remove every trace of Tobias from her mind.

In the present, the clinic's receptionist, Rosa, emptied the filing cabinets, quit her job, and posted the files and session tapes back to every patient on the books.

Rosa’s betrayal was born of the very chain of events Tobias had set off. After Ivy's erasure, Tobias had visited her bookshop to reconcile, only to find her treating him like a complete stranger while flirting with a young clerk named Peck. When his friends Nina and Grady showed him the clinic's standard form letter explaining her missing memory, Tobias had rushed to Dr. Hallam demanding the exact same procedure, promptly packing two carrier bags of mementos so the clinic could map the attached recollections.

Sitting together on the flat's stairwell, Tobias and Ivy pressed play on the tape Rosa had mailed. They listened in sickened silence to their own recorded voices tearing each other apart. Overwhelmed, Ivy ran down the stairs, but after a moment in the cold air, she returned, sat beside him, and agreed to try again anyway.

Everything had culminated on the night of Tobias's procedure. Technicians Dell and Peck had set up the equipment in his flat, Peck quietly pocketing the boxed keepsakes to use on Ivy later. As the machine ran backwards, dissolving the recent, ugly memories of shouting and smashed metal, Tobias had changed his mind in his sleep, trying frantically to smuggle Ivy into childhood kitchens where she had never been. Dell and Rosa had gotten high on his bed and ignored the failing map until Dr. Hallam rushed in to re-map the mindscape. In the hallway, Rosa kissed the director, only for Hallam's wife to step out of the shadows and reveal that Rosa's own affair with Hallam had been systematically erased from her mind. Inside the machine's final surviving memory—the shuttered house on the shore—Ivy’s fading projection had held Tobias's hand and spoken her last command before the void took over: "Meet me at the beach."

Nadir stood in the gun shop while the dealer mimicked his accent for an audience of no one. Sahar translated in a flat voice, her shoulder touching her father’s, until they walked out into the cold holding a small black box and a heavy paper bag.

Across town, Trey and Kwame stepped onto the pavement outside an upscale restaurant, drew handguns, and took a prosecutor named Halstead’s car straight off the curb while Halstead and his wife stared.

That same evening, Officer Boyle pulled over Clay and Renee Hobart for a nonexistent infraction. Boyle made them stand against the hood, sliding a thick hand up Renee’s skirt under the pretext of a search while Clay stood three feet away, terrified and motionless, saying nothing. His partner, Voss, watched from the cruiser.

***

Rain lashed the windshield weeks later when Voss pulled over to pick up a young man hitchhiking by the highway. They talked casually for a mile, until the passenger reached into his jacket pocket. Driven by sudden panic, Voss pulled his service weapon and fired two rounds into the boy’s chest. Hours later, he stood in the dark watching the car burn near a muddy drainage ditch.

***

The morning after the traffic stop, Voss walked into his commander’s office and requested a new patrol car, agreeing to lie that Boyle’s severe flatulence was the reason he could no longer ride with him.

Locksmith Mateo arrived at the Halstead residence to change the front door locks. From the landing above, Paula Halstead shouted down to her husband that the tattooed man would be selling their house keys to gang members before morning. 

Mateo left there and went to Nadir’s ruined storefront. He replaced the lock cylinder, then pointed out that the wooden frame was completely splintered—the lock meant nothing if the door wasn't replaced. Nadir spat on the threshold, accusing Mateo of inventing work to scam a desperate man.

Meanwhile, Boyle sat across a desk from a health insurance clerk named Delia Frank, pleading for a medical referral for his dying, incontinent father. When Delia coldly refused, Boyle screamed at her nametag until security escorted him out.

That night, Nadir’s shop was smashed open and looted down to the bare shelves. The insurance adjuster reviewed the report and denied the claim entirely because Nadir had ignored the locksmith’s explicit warning.

Disaster struck again when Renee Hobart was pinned upside down in a rollover wreck, petrol dripping toward a growing fire. It was Boyle who crawled through the shattered glass, sliced her seatbelt, and dragged her clear seconds before the vehicle exploded.

In another part of the city, Trey and Kwame ran down a small man named Pham as he crossed between parked delivery vans. They argued violently, finally dumping his broken body at an emergency room entrance. 

When Clay Hobart tried to drive his own vehicle later that week, four officers swarmed him at gunpoint, believing the car stolen. As Clay screamed in rage, Voss walked into the middle of the standoff and talked the officers down, saving Clay's life. Clay then sped away with Trey cowering in his passenger seat, eventually pulling over on a dark verge and shoving Trey out into the night without a word.

Consuming himself with vengeance, Nadir waited outside Mateo’s house with his new pistol. When Mateo stepped onto the porch, Nadir raised the gun and shouted. Just as he pulled the trigger, Mateo’s small daughter, Rosie, sprinted into her father's arms. But the weapon only popped softly—Sahar had secretly purchased blanks. Unharmed, Nadir fell to his knees, believing the child was an angel sent to save his soul.

Later that rainy night, Voss picked up Kwame hitchhiking by the highway, panicked when Kwame reached for his pocket, shot him dead, and burned the patrol car.

Detective Isaiah Reece was called out to a muddy roadside the next morning, walking up to a body face down in the ditch. He froze, recognizing his brother Kwame's shoes. At home, their mother collapsed on the kitchen floor, weeping and blaming Isaiah for never once going to look for him.

Paula Halstead fell down her grand staircase while alone, lying helpless until her housekeeper Alba found her. In the ambulance, Paula clutched Alba’s hand, sobbing that Alba was the only true friend she had.

Trey bought Pham’s wrecked van cheap at an impound yard. Opening the back expecting cargo, he discovered two dozen terrified trafficked migrants. Remembering the man who had spared him, Trey drove them to the docks, gave them all the cash in his pockets, and set them free.

As the first snow began to fall, two cars collided at a slippery intersection, and both drivers stepped out into the freeze, shouting before either had even inspected the damage.

Ruben shared a cramped, suffocating house with his mother, his brother Nestor, Nestor’s wife Alma, and her baby. When Nestor robbed a pharmacy by night and came home to beat Alma across the kitchen, Ruben urged her to run away with him. He financed their escape after discovering that Nestor’s rottweiler, Tigre, killed other dogs on sight, steadily accumulating cash by entering the dog in local fights. Desperate to remove his brother, Ruben paid two thugs in a bar to beat Nestor. But Nestor guessed the truth, seized all of Ruben’s hidden savings, and disappeared with Alma and the child. Later, during a final match, the promoter Chaco shot Tigre in the ring; Ruben stabbed Chaco in revenge and fled in a truck with his friend Pipo. Blasting through a red light at high speed, Ruben ploughed directly into another car. Months afterward, when Nestor was shot dead attempting to rob a bank, Ruben attended the funeral and offered Alma a fresh start one last time, but she looked at him and refused.

Before the collision, the model Celine Vaz had moved into a plush new flat facing a massive billboard carrying her own face, provided by her lover Hector, who had abandoned his wife and daughters at a birthday party. Celine woke in a hospital bed with her shattered leg pinned together by steel cages, asking instantly about her lapdog Chispa. Left alone in the empty flat, Chispa had fallen through a hole in the floorboards and could not climb back out. As Celine’s neglected leg turned gangrenous back in the ward, Hector frantically tore up the apartment's floorboards one by one with a crowbar to locate the whining dog. The leg was ultimately amputated above the knee. In that same week, workmen stripped down the giant billboard across the street, leaving Celine and Hector sitting together in a demolished apartment, staring out at a blank frame.

At the junction during the crash, Cardo—a former guerrilla turned vagrant contract killer—stood amidst the smoke and dragged the bleeding Tigre out of the wreck. He nursed the dog back to health over weeks in a yard full of strays, feeding him by hand until Tigre recovered. Meanwhile, a businessman named Elian paid Cardo half in advance to assassinate his half-brother and business partner, Sergio. Around the same time, Cardo watched quietly from a distance as his estranged wife was buried by relatives who thought he had died decades ago, then trailed his grown daughter Perla back to her building. Returning to his yard, Cardo discovered Tigre had slaughtered every other stray dog in the pack; he pressed a loaded pistol against the dog's head, but found himself unable to pull the trigger. Instead of killing Sergio as contracted, Cardo abducted him off the pavement and chained him to a bed frame in his empty kennels. He then brought Elian face to face with his captive brother, placed a loaded pistol on the floor between them, collected payment from both, and walked away. Cardo broke into Perla’s flat while she was at work, left a long confession on her answering machine detailing who he was, took her photograph from a shelf, shaved, put on clean clothes, left his collected money on her table, and walked out into the flat grey wasteland accompanied only by Tigre.

For six months I had not slept properly. The only cure was an hour in church basements weeping among the terminally ill, held by strangers who believed I was dying too. Then Ada Vey started showing up to the same groups. She smoked through the meditations and faked her tears so blatantly that she exposed the lie in both of us. My relief evaporated, and the insomnia returned.

Later, in the darkness of a high-rise service stairwell, Rex would beat me down flight after flight. Standing at the bottom with blood in my eyes, I would understand that the gun in his hand was actually in my own. I would press the cold steel barrel past my teeth, angle it toward my cheek, and pull the trigger.

On a late-night flight, I sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow. He spent forty minutes explaining how everything we owned had been chosen for us by catalogues, then handed me his business card. When an explosion blew the windows of my flat onto the pavement and turned my catalogue furniture to ash, I called Rex from a phone box. He brought me to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district. 

Outside a bar that night, Rex asked me to hit him as hard as I could. We beat each other bloody on the car park tarmac until neither could stand. That private brawl hardened into a weekly basement club with strict rules, drawing in hundreds of men desperate to feel something real.

When Ada overdosed on pills, Rex brought her back to the derelict house. Soon, their loud affair echoed through every floor while I lay rigid downstairs. To fund us, Rex stole bags of fat from the yard of a cosmetic surgery clinic, rendered it down into luxury soap on the kitchen stove, and sold it back to department stores at eighty dollars a bar. During one burn, Rex held my wet hand flat on the table and poured lye onto my skin, refusing to let me retreat into meditation. I used my ruined, beaten face to blackmail my employer, forcing him to pay my salary just to stay away.

Rex transformed the club into Project Havoc. The house filled with shaven-headed recruits who took orders, slept on the floor, and vandalized corporate property at night. Then, during a rainstorm, Rex took both hands off the wheel, steered us into oncoming traffic, let the car roll into a ditch, and vanished.

When a recruit named Ogden was shot dead by police during a midnight raid, I set out across the country to shut the operation down. In every city, I found identical cellar clubs with the same rules posted on the walls. Barmen and desk clerks recognized me instantly, greeting me as Rex Marrow. 

In a quiet motel room, staring at airline receipts and flight logs, the truth coalesced: there was no separate soap salesman. One body, one bank account. Rex was acting during the hours I thought I was asleep. I called Ada, and her tired voice confirmed it—she had been sleeping with me the entire time.

Searching for the final objective, I discovered Havoc had placed tons of explosives in the subterranean garages beneath the debt-record companies, intending to erase the world’s financial ledgers. I ran into the towers to disarm the charges.

In the darkness of the high-rise service stairwell, Rex beat me down flight after flight. Standing at the bottom with blood in my eyes, I understood that the gun in his hand was actually in my own. I pressed the cold steel barrel past my teeth, angled it toward my cheek, and pulled the trigger. 

The shot blew through my face, killing the illusion of Rex forever. Minutes later, two shaven recruits brought Ada into the room, apologized, and stepped back. My face wrapped in soaked bandages, I took Ada’s hand at the window. Together, we watched the financial towers collapse one by one into the dust.

Disguised as devout pilgrims, Solly Two Coats and his crew robbed a northern port diamond house, slipping past the security guards and walking out with a magnificent stone. Overseas, his cousin Marv placed a terse phone call ordering Solly to bring the rock straight over without delay. But back in the city, Grigor the Nail directed Solly toward a local bookmaker’s to lay a wager, while secretly tipping off pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to rob Solly at that very location.

Meanwhile, boxing promoters Halloway and Digby dispatched their contracted fighter, Pretty Sam, to purchase a caravan from a camp of travellers. A dispute flared up over the deal, and Finn, an unlicensed bare-knuckle fighter from the camp, knocked Sam out cold. The blow left Halloway abruptly without a man for gang boss Coldstone’s fixed bout. Cornered, Halloway entered Finn into the fight instead, promising Coldstone that Finn would dutifully go down in the fourth round.

Upon landing in the city, Solly promptly delivered the stolen diamond to the fence Hersch for safekeeping. Carrying only an empty leather case, he headed to the bookmaker's. As planned by Grigor's double-dealing tip-off, Ike, Benno, and Tulley attempted the robbery. They bungled it horribly in the chaos, seizing Solly’s arm and his case before being chased off by Grigor himself. That night, Finn ignored the fixed instructions completely and knocked his opponent out cold in the very first round. Coldstone lost a vast fortune on the wager and brutally took his frustration out on Halloway.

Marv flew into the city, found Solly missing, and immediately hired the ruthless bounty hunter Ledge to track his cousin down. Elsewhere, Grigor seized Solly and cut off his arm to force open the stolen case, only to discover to his fury that the diamond was not inside. Ledge tracked the pawnbrokers down after they had retrieved the stone from Hersch; he shot their car to pieces and commandeered both the captured men and the jewel. Coldstone, oblivious to the diamond plot, fed the mutilated Solly to his pigs, using the gruesome sight to warn Halloway and Digby what would happen to them if the upcoming second fight went wrong.

Halloway and Digby once again instructed Finn to drop in the fourth round of the rematch. To guarantee obedience, Coldstone’s enforcers raided the travellers' camp and burned Finn’s mother to death inside her caravan.

On the road, Grigor ambushed Ledge’s vehicle while Ike and Benno remained trapped inside. The chaotic, point-blank shootout ended with Ledge, Grigor, and Benno all lying dead on the pavement. In the immediate aftermath, Tulley slipped away unnoticed, carrying off a stray dog that had swallowed the loose diamond during the carnage.

At the arena, Finn waited until the designated fourth round, but instead of taking a dive, he knocked his opponent out cold once again. Simultaneously, armed travellers hidden throughout the crowd drew weapons and massacred Coldstone’s men. With the mob boss exposed and his muscle destroyed, Halloway and Digby cornered Coldstone and shot him dead. By morning, the travellers had vanished without a trace.

Sometime later, the stray dog was handed in at a local pet shop, where it coughed up the brilliant diamond, leaving Halloway and Digby as the ultimate, unsuspecting holders of the prize.

Elsewhere, Grigor seized Solly and cut off his arm to force open the stolen case, only to discover to his fury that the diamond was not inside. Ledge tracked the pawnbrokers down after they had retrieved the stone from Hersch; he shot their car to pieces and commandeered both the captured men and the jewel. Coldstone, oblivious to the diamond plot, fed the mutilated Solly to his pigs, using the gruesome sight to warn Halloway and Digby what would happen to them if the upcoming second fight went wrong.

In the immediate aftermath, Tulley slipped away unnoticed, carrying off a stray dog that had swallowed the loose diamond during the carnage.

At the arena, Finn waited until the designated fourth round, but instead of taking a dive, he knocked his opponent out cold once again. Simultaneously, armed travellers hidden throughout the crowd drew weapons and massacred Coldstone’s men. With the mob boss exposed and his muscle destroyed, Halloway and Digby cornered Coldstone and shot him dead. By morning, the travellers had vanished without a trace.

Sometime later, the stray dog was handed in at a local pet shop, where it coughed up the brilliant diamond, leaving Halloway and Digby as the ultimate, unsuspecting holders of the prize.

All night, low over the urban roofs, a fleet of helicopters sprayed pest poison across the city, their steady drone echoing above every neighborhood.

By morning, Doctor Neil Hartigan and his wife Bess, a painter, began preparing for a dinner party, dressing in tense silence while nervous energy filled their home. Across town, the baker Otto Kemp took an order for a birthday cake meant for a boy named Charlie Rill. 

Shortly after, while on his way to school, young Charlie was knocked down by a car driven by Rhona, a frantic waitress. Though bruised, Charlie insisted he was fine and walked home on his own feet. Hours later, however, Charlie unexpectedly collapsed into a deep coma. His parents, Grant and Elaine, rushed him to the hospital to begin an agonizing vigil by his bed. While they waited, Grant's estranged father Duff arrived unexpectedly in the corridor, clumsily confessing a long-buried affair from decades past to break the stifling quiet. 

Back at the bakery, feeling unpaid and ignored regarding the uncollected order, Otto began making anonymous, menacing phone calls to the family’s ringing house. 

In a nearby neighborhood, Cheryl worked as a telephone-sex operator from her living room sofa, talking men through fantasies while her husband Stu sat beside her, quietly seething with resentment. To blow off steam, Stu drove out to the river on a fishing trip with three friends, where they stumbled upon a young woman’s body floating face down in the shallows. Unwilling to ruin their weekend, the men tethered the corpse to the bank with a line and continued fishing for two more days before finally telling anyone. When Vern’s wife Iris, a professional party clown, learned what the men had done, she was filled with deep disgust as she wiped off her face paint.

Meanwhile, the singer Vida performed nightly in a sultry club, entirely unaware that her cellist daughter Bee was spending her evenings playing alone at home in an empty house.

Elsewhere, Officer Rowe, who was cheating on his wife Peg with a woman named Nan, deliberately abandoned the family dog miles away to cover up one of his lies. When Nan's ex-husband Cass, a helicopter pilot, discovered she had a new man, he slipped into her house and systematically sawed her furniture to pieces in an outburst of jealousy. 

At the Hartigan residence, house-sitters Ike and Dot occupied the empty rooms, playfully posing Dot made up as a beaten corpse while taking dark photographs. 

Later, during the Hartigans' dinner party, Bess admitted to a past nude modeling session and an affair, driving Neil to drop his polite facade and make a shocking scene in front of their guests.

The following morning, Charlie died in his hospital room. Worn down by grief and furious over the harassing calls, Grant and Elaine drove straight to the bakery to confront Otto. Realizing their loss, the remorseful baker broke down, fed them warm bread, and wept alongside them.

Miles away in the hills, Stu was on a picnic with a young woman when a sudden rage overtook him, leading him to smash her head with a rock. 

Just as dusk fell, a sharp tremor shook the entire city, and by nightfall, every death, crime, and wreck from the preceding days was folded together into a single evening news bulletin.

A bright beam weapon strikes him dead the moment he finishes addressing a crowd, fulfilling the exact death he has always known would arrive. Long before or after, a fellow prisoner makes a solemn promise to arrange his murder to settle an old score regarding a dead scout. That scout had died of gangrene inside a crowded prison train, spending his last breath cursing the weak companion who had been captured alongside him. Before their capture, while lost behind enemy lines, the scout had repeatedly beaten him for pleading to be left in the snow to die.

In a disused abattoir in a great city, he is housed below ground in a refrigerated meat locker with other captives. A firestorm destroys the entire city in a single night, but the men inside the meat locker come up to find the world above them flattened into white ash. Captors force the survivors to dig through collapsed cellars, excavating bodies until one of the diggers dies of the dry heaves amidst the rot.

He sits in a radio studio, speaking into a microphone about the fourth dimension and the visitors who carried him away. On their distant world, the aliens keep him in a transparent zoo enclosure alongside a famous film actress. The captors explain that time does not pass, that every moment exists simultaneously, and that free will is merely an illusion peculiar to Earth. Hearing his broadcast, his daughter decides he has become senile and legally takes control of his personal affairs.

In a hospital ward, another patient introduces him to the cheap paperbacks of a hack science fiction writer. He has arrived in the ward after returning home from the war, where he collapsed completely. He had been conscripted as a chaplain’s assistant and shipped overseas with no training worth mentioning. 

In another pocket of existence, he marries the daughter of the man who owns an optometry school, entering a prosperous life that makes him wealthy. In mountain snow, rescue workers pull him alive from the wreckage of a plane crash; elsewhere on the road, his wife dies of exhaust fumes inside her idling car while driving toward the hospital where he is taken.

In a prison camp, enemy officers remain plump and healthy, having drawn double rations for years because of a lingering clerical error. In a small industrial town, a weak and peculiar boy is born into the world. His father throws the boy into the deep end of a public pool to force him to swim, but the child merely sinks to the bottom, perfectly content to remain beneath the water.

Above the street, at an open window of a high flat, an old man leaned out toward the cool night air. He was explaining to a younger man beside him that nothing anybody does survives time—and that this was not a complaint, but a simple, immutable fact.

Below that window, flashing blue light swept across the pavement. Police officers handcuffed two men and carried them out into the street. One shouted uselessly into the night; the other was entirely silent, staring into nothing as they were bundled toward a waiting van.

Inside the basement club moments before, Jonah had hauled a heavy red fire extinguisher off the wall and brought it down into a man’s face, swinging again and again long after the body on the floor had stopped moving. A few feet away, watching calmly alongside the horrified crowd, stood the pimp known as the Adder—the real rapist, completely untouched.

Cort had dragged them both into the mess after hunting desperately through the dark club, pulling faces out of the shadows until he seized a man by the shoulder. But the man he grabbed was the wrong one, and he took Cort’s arm at the elbow and turned it until the bone snapped with a sickening crack.

Earlier in the street, two touts had stepped out of a shadowed doorway. For a handful of crumpled notes, they offered to sell Cort the rapist’s name and location, steering him and Jonah down toward the subterranean entrance of the club called the Pit.

Before those men approached them, Cort and Jonah had come out of a house party still half-laughing, only to stop dead on the pavement. An ambulance stood with its doors wide and lights spinning, and on the stretcher being loaded inside was a bloodied face they both recognized.

Hours prior, deep in a pedestrian underpass, the Adder had forced Lise to the cold concrete floor and raped her. When he was finished, he smashed her head against the stone again and again, while a passer-by at the far end of the tunnel peered in, shuddered, and backed away into the dark.

Lise had descended into the tunnel only to avoid crossing four lanes of relentless night traffic. Halfway through the tiled underpass, she had walked directly upon the Adder holding a transsexual woman by her hair, beating her mercilessly with a heavy fist.

She had been walking home alone because Cort had ruined the party. He had gotten steadily drunk and high, openly pursuing other women across the room until a disgusted Lise collected her coat and walked out by herself.

Earlier that evening, Lise, Cort, and Jonah had stood swaying together in a bright underground train carriage, arguing cheerfully about sex and how much Cort had already had to drink—the easy, noisy argument of people who fully expected to be doing the same thing tomorrow.

That afternoon, the day had been entirely untouched. Sprinklers turned over cut grass in the park while children ran shrieking through the cold spray, and Lise lay on her side on the lawn with an unread book, one hand resting flat and protective against her stomach.

Before going to the park, she had sat alone on the edge of the bathtub in her quiet flat. She held a plastic stick in both hands, looking down at the positive result, and allowed herself a private, hopeful smile before telling a single soul.

And in the morning light filtering through thin curtains, Lise had lain in bed beside Cort, describing a recurring dream of a long red tunnel she was frightened to enter, while the two of them traded lazy, affectionate jokes about Jonah, her ex-boyfriend who was now their closest friend.

Emlyn sat in Wilder’s drawing room that evening, unbuttoning his coat with slow deliberation. He looked at his oldest friend and stated calmly that he had known about the affair for four full years. Odile had told him everything during their holiday abroad, he explained, adding with a cold, offhand smile that he had never thought much of Wilder’s prose in those intercepted letters either.

Hours earlier, Wilder had telephoned Emlyn in a frantic state. Stunned and trembling, he had insisted his friend come to the house immediately, unable to endure the evening alone with the strange news he had received.

The phone call had been triggered by a stray detail Odile had dropped moments before: Emlyn had quietly spent the past year publishing a novelist whom Wilder represented—a hack author both men had secretly despised for years.

They had been sitting in the quiet corner of a neighborhood bar when Odile delivered her news. Two years after she and Wilder had brought their own hidden relationship to a close, she announced that her marriage was officially over. She explained that she had spent the previous night spilling the whole truth to Emlyn, believing she was finally clearing her conscience.

Years before that bar meeting, the lovers had reached a far simpler end. Finding that their secret life had hardened into an exhausting chore, Wilder and Odile had methodically split up their small collection of crockery, packed away the linens, and surrendered the lease to the quiet flat they had shared.

Months before they gave up the apartment, Wilder had dined at the couple's home. Across the dinner table, Emlyn and Wilder had become so thoroughly absorbed in discussing boyhood racquet games and boarding-school athletics that Odile was left completely silent, alienated from the talk in her own dining room.

Earlier that same year, Emlyn had invited Wilder to an interminable, liquor-soaked restaurant lunch. Over course after course, Emlyn had relentlessly baited the agent about contemporary fiction and commercial publishing, mocking his professional judgment while carefully suppressing any mention of the secret he held.

Before that lunch took place, Odile had arrived at the rented apartment directly from her trip abroad. She had offered no details about the journey, keeping her mouth shut as the afternoon slipped by in the usual, familiar rhythm of their routine.

Yet thousands of miles away, in the quiet bedroom of a foreign hotel, she had wept and admitted everything to her husband. Emlyn had received her confession without shouting, merely observing that he had always been significantly fonder of his friend than of his wife.

That confession had been set in motion at the hotel front desk, where Emlyn had intercepted an envelope held under Odile's name. Holding it up in the lobby, he had quietly asked her about the letter, pointing out that he recognised the handwriting on the front instantly as belonging to Wilder.

Prior to that trip abroad, Odile had sat on the edge of the bed in their rented flat and broken the news that she was carrying her husband’s child. Neither she nor Wilder had suggested breaking off their meetings; instead, they resolved that the rooms would go on exactly as before.

They had rented those quiet rooms together long before the pregnancy, choosing an unassuming district far from their usual haunts. They had spent afternoons filling the cupboards with folded linens and ceramic plates, carefully bestowing upon their betrayal a domestic routine of its own.

The entire affair had started years earlier, downstairs from where it would eventually unravel. During a loud party thrown at his best friend’s house, Wilder, a rising book agent, had taken Odile by the wrist, pulled her away from the laughter into a quiet upstairs bedroom, and told her just how lovely she was while the rest of the company drank below.
